1:
Ellicott opens with a difficulty of sources: the three parables of this chapter follow naturally on the preceding discourse, yet neither Mark nor Luke shows any trace of them being spoken then, which he thinks calls for explanation, and he suggests the apocalyptic teaching was impressed orally as the fall of Jerusalem drew near and written down afterwards with the variations such a process brings. Clarke refers the parable to two periods at once, the destruction of Jerusalem and the last judgment. Gill takes the kingdom here for the Gospel church state and notes the connection with the chapter before, while doubting that the church was drowsy in the years before the Jewish ruin. Barnes explains why a wedding serves the purpose, the marriage bond being the most tender relation known on earth.

On the properties of the scene two witnesses supply what a modern reader lacks. Robertson says there is no special point in the number and describes the lamps as torches, a wooden staff with a dish on top holding rope or cloth soaked in oil, while allowing that the word can mean a household lamp. Lightfoot answers the number from Jewish custom, since a synagogue required ten, and an order of men required ten, the ring formed about mourners on returning from a burial being of ten at the least.

The fathers divide over what the oil stands for. Chrysostom makes it mercy and almsgiving, and draws the sharp conclusion that virginity unaccompanied by works of mercy is cast out with the adulterers, the foolish having lost the greater labour for want of the less. Augustine reads the five as a fivefold continence from the pleasures of eye, ear, smell, taste and touch, and makes the oil gladness, so that a man whose joy comes from pleasing God inwardly carries oil, while one who is continent for the praise of men has none. Calvin will have none of the older use of the passage, calling it a childish speculation to adduce it in praise of virginity, since the aim is only to lessen the uneasiness caused by delay.

The two epithets are examined by Clarke, who prefers provident to wise and careless to foolish, citing a lexicon which defines the second word as one who does not see what is necessary; the want, he says, was of the salvation of God in the soul behind the burning lamp of profession. Ellicott identifies the oil more definitely as the gift of the Spirit, without which the torch first burns dim and then goes out. Gill produces a rabbinic parable of a king who summoned his servants without naming the hour, the wise adorning themselves and waiting at the palace gate while the foolish went about their business, and Lightfoot cites the same story. Barnes enters a caution against pressing the arithmetic, since nothing can be argued from the proportion about how many professors are sincere.

The sleeping divides them again. Calvin rejects both the reading that makes it sloth and the reading that makes it death, and takes it simply for the earthly occupations in which believers must be engaged while they remain in the body. Barnes agrees that the detail is there to establish the duty of readiness and not to assert that none will be ready. Lightfoot supplies an old definition of a slumberer, a man who sleeps and does not sleep, who will answer yes or no if called but cannot answer anything that needs thought. Robertson catches the change of tense, a nodding off followed by continued sleep, and observes that many a preacher has watched it happen. Wesley makes the distinction fall not on the sleep but on the peace, the wise enjoying a true one and the foolish a false.
6:
The hour is made to carry weight. Clarke notes that Jewish weddings were held at night but usually began at the rising of the evening star, so this delay is more than ordinary; Wesley calls it an hour quite unthought of; Ellicott sees a hint of a like lateness in the true Bridegroom's coming, and reads the cry as answering to the stir that announces any crisis in a church or a people. Robertson catches the tense, a cry has come, the perfect keeping the memory of the outcry alive with all its bustle. Calvin takes the noise for a sudden arrival, adding that at the last the whole frame of the world will resound so as to wake not only sleepers but the dead. Henry answers why the tarrying was needed: the elect must be called in, God's patience shown, the saints' patience tried, the harvest of earth and heaven ripened; yet though Christ tarry past our time he will not tarry past the due time.

On the trimming, Barnes explains the action, the burnt linen removed and the wick dipped again, and finds a picture of men making ready only at the approach of death, alarmed and asking help when it is too late. Clarke describes eastern lamps he has seen, skeletons of wood and thread covered with fine gauze and painted with flowers, though the word may mean no more than preparing them to burn.

The failing lamps are read closely. Ellicott and Robertson both insist on the present tense, are going out rather than are gone out, the flax still smoking; Robertson adds that outward religion is found to have no illuminating power at the moment it is called on. Clarke presses it the other way, that lamps going out were once lighted, so these had hearts once warmed and let the light become darkness. Gill observes that a graceless person may see and acknowledge grace in others, which is what the request amounts to.

The refusal is handled with care by several. Ellicott notes that the words not so are supplied by the translators, and hears in the original a regretful tenderness that gives the reason without uttering a refusal. Wesley admires the abruptness of the sentence and answers the question himself, that there is not enough, since no man has more holiness than he needs. Clarke draws the consequence bluntly: nobody has merit to bequeath, and no work of supererogation can be placed to another's account. Calvin allows that gifts are ordinarily distributed so members may aid one another, and says the parable points to the moment when each stands at the tribunal carrying his own bundle. Gill is careful that the denial sprang neither from want of compassion nor from a niggardly spirit.

What the door shut means, all agree, and they press it hard. Ellicott says the mistake lay in not going earlier, since it is too late at the crisis to begin forming character by ordinances and rules of life. Robertson renders the aorist shut to stay shut. Clarke observes that earnest prayer used in time may do much, yet this parable shows a time may come when prayer even to Jesus is too late. Barnes cautions that the later knocking is not to be pressed into a doctrine of applicants after the judgment. On the sentence Barnes and Clarke agree that to know here means to acknowledge and approve. Gregory reads the failing lamps as works that looked bright to men and are found dark before God, and takes the arising of all the virgins for the rousing of elect and reprobate alike from the sleep of death. Origen makes the oil the word of teaching stored in the vessel of the soul. Gill and Wesley end where the parable does, on watching, Wesley noting that the watcher sleeps too, yet his heart wakes: quiet, but not secure.
14:
Whether this is the parable of the pounds told again is settled at once. Ellicott grants many points in common with the story in Luke but finds the distinctive features of each marked enough to require separate handling. Lightfoot makes the difference concrete: there the sums are pounds and here talents, and the occasions differ, the one spoken on the road up from Jericho before Lazarus was raised, this one seated on the mount three days before the Passover. Robertson agrees they are not variants of one story and adds a barb, that some scholars credit Jesus with very little versatility.

The journey draws the two patristic readings. Gregory takes the traveller for the Redeemer ascending in the flesh he had assumed, since the proper home of flesh is earth and it goes abroad when placed in heaven. Origen guards the same point against misuse: the travelling belongs to the dispensation of the flesh and not to the divine nature, for he who promised to be with them always is not circumscribed by bodily form; and he is careful to say that in distinguishing thus we do not divide Jesus but assign to each substance its own properties. He notices too that the parable does not begin I am like, because the traveller stands for the man and not the Son of God.

What the sums were worth is variously reckoned. Gill gives two authorities, one making a silver talent about three hundred and seventy-five pounds and a gold one four thousand five hundred, the other raising both, so that five talents come to eighteen hundred and seventy-five pounds in silver or twenty-two thousand five hundred in gold, a very large trust for one servant. Barnes converts to dollars and takes the figure to denote the highest abilities and the greatest opportunity of doing good. Ellicott turns instead to the English word, noting that the modern languages of Europe bear witness in their use of it to the impression this parable made, and that the common sense of the term, and the ill-coined adjective formed from it, tend to obscure what the parable actually means.

On the unequal distribution the comment is unanimous but variously grounded. Clarke says God never makes men proprietors of his goods, who hold them only so long as it pleases their Lord, and adds that to give eminent gifts to persons incapable of improving them would be to lay a snare. Calvin refuses to divide natural endowments from the gifts of the Spirit, since neither power nor skill is anything but received, so that a man who allows God his share leaves nothing for himself. Barnes says God assigns the station he judges each fitted to fill. Wesley wonders whether the disproportion between those who receive most and least is really greater than this, renders the phrase according to his own mighty power, and glosses the departure as a journey to heaven. Gregory allegorises the sums as the five senses, then understanding and action, then understanding alone.

The trading and the burying are set against each other. Robertson marks the promptness of the first servant, notes that his gain was a hundred per cent, and quotes the summary that the virgins wait while the servants work. Ellicott finds it strikingly suggestive that the two larger trusts were faithfully used and the smallest was not, and explains it as true to human nature, since the presence of wide opportunity itself brings a sense of responsibility, so that failure there is rarer though its condemnation is greater. Barnes lists the pleas by which the neglect is defended, that the station is humble, the abilities slender, and the portion smaller than another's, and dismisses all three. Wesley turns the last of them on the reader directly, asking whether he is hiding the talent God has lent him.
19:
The long interval is read as deliberate. Ellicott hears in it, as in the parable before, a faint suggestion of a delay longer than men looked for in the coming it answers to. Henry denies that the deferral implies slackness, since everything must be done in its own time and order, and says the stewards of the manifold grace of God must shortly account for it. Gill spreads the reckoning across several occasions, a fit of illness, a season of persecution, the hour of death, or finally the judgment, when ministers no less than others must answer for the gifts they received. Barnes defines the term simply as settling accounts and inquiring into faithfulness. Robertson contributes a point of usage: the phrase is a business idiom, found in the papyri and on a Nubian potsherd but absent from the classical writers, which makes it the language of the counting-house rather than of literature.

Calvin defends the image itself. The life of believers is justly compared to trade, since men are meant to exchange and barter with one another so that intercourse is maintained, and the industry with which each discharges his office, the calling itself, and the power of acting well are so many kinds of merchandise, because their object is mutual usefulness. What Christ means by gain, he says, is general usefulness. Ellicott makes the same correction from the other side, that in the kingdom of God the increase seldom appears as more gifts and opportunities, though even that may follow faithfulness, but as good done to men and souls gained for God.

Over the commendation Gill enters a caveat worth keeping. Ministers do not say well done to themselves; knowing they can do nothing well of themselves, they own that when all is done they are unprofitable servants, and they neither expect nor seek such praise from men; the word is spoken to show how acceptable a laborious ministry is to Christ and to encourage industry in it. Chrysostom narrows the adjective, taking the goodness commended to be goodness shown toward a neighbour, and reads the joy as a word for complete blessedness.

The promotion is where Ellicott finds most. He corrects the English first, since the word ruler is not in the Greek and the sense is simply that the servant will be set over many things; then he takes the clause as a glimpse behind the veil. The reward of faithful work lies not in rest only but in enlarged activity, so that the world to come is joined to this one by a law of continuity, and those who have used their gifts to turn many to righteousness may find new spheres for the same work. Barnes reads the joy either as the festivity of the master's return or as the reward prepared beforehand, and Robertson inclines to the feast.

The second servant receives the identical words, and Henry draws the encouragement out of that fact. The returns were proportioned to the receipts throughout: from the man given five, five are expected, and the greater the gifts the more pains are owed, as a large stock demands more management; but from the man given two, only two are looked for. That, he says, may hearten anyone placed in a lower and narrower sphere of usefulness, since whoever lays himself out to do good according to the best of his capacity and opportunity is accepted, even though he does not do so much good as another. Gill makes the same point by noting that the second man is reckoned with next because he traded next, and in proportion to what he had received gained as truly as the first.
24:
Ellicott puts the excuse as a question with two answers. Either the plea was an afterthought got up to cover what had been plain sloth, in which case the lesson is that neglect of loyal service soon breeds disloyal thoughts; or the man had cherished that estimate of his master all along, and it was the root of the neglect. Robertson notes that the word for hard is rougher than the term Luke uses, grasping and ungenerous, and that the scattering in view is the winnowing of chaff rather than the sowing of seed. Wesley answers the charge outright, that the man knew nothing of the sort, since no one who thinks God a hard master ever knew him, and that every obstinate sinner contrives in some fashion to lay his own sins at God's door. Barnes states the purpose of this third case: having few talents excuses no one.

The alleged fear satisfies none of them. Ellicott calls it simulated rather than real, since genuine fear would have driven the man away from unfaithful service, and finds under it a taunt, that he dared risk nothing for a master who made no allowance for good intentions. Gill agrees the fear was the pretence and names the true causes, sloth and earthly mindedness. Barnes says it expresses exactly how sinners regard God, and that all their excuses are excuses for indolence. Wesley presses it into the present tense, that from just this fear one man will not learn to read and another will not hear sermons.

The reply about the bankers is where the commentary is thickest. Lightfoot reads it as argument turned back on the speaker: the lord never meant his money to be put out at interest but traded honestly, and answers only in terms the servant had himself supplied, since a man who thinks his master griping might at least have used the gain that suits such a character. Ellicott explains the word as counter-keepers, bankers having originally been those who sat at a bench, and prefers interest to usury, the term implying nothing illegal in itself; Clarke agrees, rendering it the money's produce and reserving usury for unlawful gain. Gill gives the Jewish name and notes that the Eastern versions read put my money on the table. Robertson observes that the excuse convicts the man out of his own mouth. Origen raises a question the others do not, whether all men are the king's servants or only those foreknown, and whether the bankers stand outside that number altogether.

The transfer of the talent Ellicott takes as decisive for interpretation: abilities cannot be handed from one man to another, but opportunities can and constantly are, so the talents must be the external openings given for the use of ability. He illustrates the law stated next from ordinary life, that non-user tends to invalidate a legal right and an unexercised muscle degenerates. Gill draws a different inference from the same removal, that the talent cannot mean saving grace, since the gift and calling of that are without repentance, whereas gifts may fail and be taken away. Henry notes the man neither embezzled nor squandered but simply hid, and quotes Bacon that money is like manure, good for nothing in the heap and needing to be spread.

On the sentence Wesley is the most arresting. What had the man done? Not good, certainly; but he is charged with no harm either, and for barely doing no harm he is sent into the dark, so that the mere harmlessness on which many build their hope of salvation was the cause of his damnation. Robertson says the same in four words, that doing nothing is doing harm. Calvin explains the darkness by the setting, since banquets were held at night under many lamps, so that those shut out are cast into the night outside the lit house.
31:
Ellicott begins by denying the usual label. We speak of the sheep and the goats as a parable, but from its opening the passage moves out of parable into plain declaration, the animals serving only as a subordinate illustration dropped into the middle; the form of the announcement rests on the vision in Daniel. Wesley responds to the manner rather than the matter, calling it one of the noblest instances of the true sublime, equalled by few descriptions even in Scripture. Barnes gives three reasons for referring it to the last judgment rather than the fall of Jerusalem: it answers a question about the end of the world, all nations are assembled, which did not happen at Jerusalem, and a separation is made between righteous and wicked which did not happen there either.

Who is gathered divides them sharply. Ellicott presses the Greek, which with the article almost always marks the heathen peoples as distinguished from Israel, and makes that the key to the whole section. Robertson denies it flatly: the phrase covers Jews as well as Gentiles, Christians and non-Christians alike. Gill takes a third line, that although the words are true of every individual who ever lived, the passage concerns professors of the Christian religion, since the two preceding parables did. Clarke stands nearest Robertson, reading it of the Gentile world with the Jews necessarily included. Robertson adds a defence of the passage itself against those who treat it as the evangelist's composition designed to exalt Christ, asking why he should not have said it if he was what he claimed, and remarking that a reduced Christ has trouble with all the Gospels and not merely the fourth.

On the manner of the coming the fathers are more speculative. Augustine holds that the wicked and the righteous alike will see him in the human shape he took from us, and that only afterwards will he be seen in the form of God which believers long for. Origen expects the body to be as it was in the transfiguration, offers two readings of the throne, either the more perfect among the saints or certain angelic powers, and denies the gathering need be local at all: the nations will simply no longer be scattered among false opinions about him, since his divinity will be so manifest that not even sinners can be ignorant of it, which is what the comparison with lightning was meant to convey. Calvin turns it to use, that believers should contemplate with the eyes of faith a heavenly life now hidden, set against the disorders of present warfare.

The attendants raise a smaller question. Clarke notes that the word holy before angels is missing from many manuscripts and was struck from the text by Griesbach, and mentions the supposition that other messengers besides the holy ones may attend. Augustine offers a bolder reading, that the angels here may be men who judge with Christ, since the word means messenger and is rightly applied to all who have brought tidings of salvation.

The imagery of the last two verses is filled in from custom. Clarke observes that sheep and goats were never penned together, though they might graze the same pasture in separate flocks, and quotes a Latin eclogue for the practice; on the hands he gathers the rabbinic usage in which the right means approbation and the left rejection, and notes that the Romans used the same emblem. Barnes makes the sheep stand for harmlessness and the right hand for honour. Gill identifies the sheep as those the Father gave to Christ. Gregory sorts the whole scene into four classes, those judged who reign, those not judged who reign, unbelievers who perish without examination since their unbelief has condemned them already, and those who profess the faith without the works of it and are convicted in order to be condemned.
34:
Ellicott corrects the address: the Greek says not blessed by my Father but ye blessed ones who belong to my Father, and he presses the scope of what follows, that the kingdom was prepared not for Israel only, nor only for those who believed in this life, but for all who in every nation feared God and wrought righteousness. Barnes glosses the preparation as designed beforehand, and Robertson refers it to the eternal purpose of the Father for his elect among all the nations. Wesley adds a speculation, wondering whether a kingdom prepared on purpose for these implies that man was not created merely to fill the places of the fallen angels.

Whether the works are the cause of the reward is met head on. Calvin concedes that if Christ were speaking of the cause of salvation his opponents could not be blamed for inferring merit; but the design is exhortation, so nothing can be concluded here about the value of works, and the stress laid on the connecting word is weak, since eternal life promised to the righteous need not imply a cause. Gill reaches the same place by another road, that these acts are not causes of the kingdom being prepared but descriptions of character, evidences of a grace already given. Clarke states the balance: whatever is done for Christ is done through Christ's grace, the doer ascribing to him both the will and the power and expecting the kingdom not as wages but as unmerited gift.

The list itself is examined. Ellicott counts six of the seven corporal works of mercy of later Christian ethics, the missing one being care of the fatherless, and notes with Robertson that the verb rendered visited is stronger than the modern English, meaning to look after, sharing a root with the word for an overseer. Clarke observes that of all the fruits of the Spirit only those springing from mercy appear here, as giving the nearest conformity to God, and cites the rabbinic saying that whoever neglects to visit the sick is as one who has shed blood. Wesley makes the sharpest point about the selection: outward mercy presupposes faith and love and must be accompanied by spiritual mercy, but the Judge could not list those in the same manner, since he could not say I was in error and ye recalled me to the truth.

Who is surprised, and why, divides them. Ellicott holds the question could not come from believers already taught this, who know what their acts of mercy signify; in the mouths of heathen before the throne it is natural, since they acted from what seemed ordinary kindness toward ordinary objects. Barnes and Wesley read it as representation rather than transcript, Barnes finding the humility of men who feel their kindness too poor to deserve praise, Wesley observing that neither party values its own works as the Judge does. Calvin says Christ represents them as doubting what they know, to set the truth vividly before their eyes.

On the last clause all converge. Barnes takes the brethren for Christians, or for the afflicted who suffer as Christ did. Clarke marvels that those whom many would scorn to set with the dogs of their flock are called the brothers and sisters of Jesus. Ellicott extends it by degrees to every member of the family of man, since the Lord who took their flesh is not ashamed to call them brethren, finding here the divine form of a sympathy that counts nothing human alien. Calvin turns it to practice, that whenever we are reluctant to help the poor we should set the Son of God before our eyes. Robertson says simply that Christ identifies himself with the suffering, and Wesley widens the encouragement from the household of faith to all men. Clarke ends smaller, that the barbarous phrase an hungered should be banished for hungry.
41:
Ellicott notices what the sentence leaves out. The blessing named the Father; the curse does not, an omission he thinks every way significant, since God is not its author, and those who have brought a curse on themselves by their own deeds are simply no longer acknowledged. Wesley fastens on the other half, that the fire was prepared for the devil and his angels and not originally for these, who are intruders into it. Clarke divides the sentence into the loss expressed by depart and the pain that follows; Barnes explains the fire as an image of extreme suffering rather than a description. Calvin observes that the threat is framed not to terrify the reprobate now, who are intoxicated with fading prosperity and think they have made a covenant with death, but to warn believers.

The recital of the omissions is read for its rhythm and its substance. Robertson says the repeated negative falls like clods on a coffin, and adds that some sheep will think themselves goats and some goats think themselves sheep. Ellicott points out that every sin named here is one of omission, opportunities common to all men left unused, as the opportunities of office were in the parable of the talents. Barnes makes that the public ground of the sentence, while allowing positive sins are not thereby excused. Clarke turns it on the reader: if men were certain Christ was somewhere in the land hungry and imprisoned they would run to relieve him, and he has said plainly that the destitute man is his representative, yet the testimony goes unregarded. Gill infers that these lived among Christians and bore the Christian name.

Their protest draws short answers. Wesley observes that self-justification will still be going on at that day. Calvin says the excuses by which they deceive themselves will be worth nothing then, their pride toward the poor coming of a supposition that it goes unpunished.

The last verse turns on a single Greek adjective, and four of them make the same argument independently. Ellicott insists the two English words render one Greek word, so the same term ought to stand in both clauses, and prefers eternal on philological grounds. Robertson allows that the noun for punishment comes from a verb meaning to prune, and that those who hold the larger hope take it as age-long discipline rather than penalty, but answers that one adjective governs both nouns, so whoever shortens the one shortens the life as well. Wesley states it as a bare alternative, that either the punishment is strictly eternal or the reward is not. Clarke says the opinion that this punishment will end is as likely as that the glory of the righteous will end. Barnes attacks from another side, against those who would punish sin rather than sinners, since persons are said to go away, and sin in the abstract cannot be punished at all.

The fathers had met the same objections. Augustine reports men deceiving themselves by allowing the fire everlasting while denying it of the punishment, and says the Lord foresaw the evasion and closed it; he adds that eternal life needs qualifying as peace in life eternal, since the wicked are immortal too. Gregory answers two arguments: to those who call the threat an empty terror meant to deter, that a God who threatens falsely to check vice must promise falsely to encourage virtue, so in proving him merciful they charge him with fraud; and to those who say finite sin cannot deserve infinite punishment, that the Judge weighs hearts and not acts only, so a heart that would never in this life be without sin may justly never be without punishment. Origen notes the order reversed, mercy recording the good first and judgment naming the punishment last, so terror may deter and honour draw. Gill ends where the chapter does: no appeal, and no higher tribunal.
